claim_as_stated: Federal civilian workforce fell from ~2.31M (Sep 2024) to ~2.04M (Jan 2026); ~317k departures in 2025 (PPS / OPM data).
correct_statement: Federal civilian workforce fell from 2,313,216 (Sep 2024) to 2,035,344 (Jan 2026), a net drop of ~278k (12%) (Partnership for Public Service, from OPM data). The ~317,000 figure for 2025 departures is OPM Director Scott Kupor's own tally (X post, Dec 10, 2025: DRP ~144k, early retirement/buyouts ~21k, routine attrition ~129k, involuntary ~24k incl. RIF ~17k and probationary ~7k; ~68k hires by end-Aug), not a PPS figure. PPS counts 386,826 separations Jan 20, 2025-Jan 2026 (incl. 136,822 DRP, 10,436 RIF).
source_title: The Federal Workforce One Year into the Trump Administration (Fed Figures); Federal workforce down 317,000 (Bloomberg via Transport Topics)
source_publisher: Partnership for Public Service; Transport Topics/Bloomberg News reporting OPM Director
note: Do not attribute 317k to PPS and do not mix the two departure counts; they cover different periods and definitions. FEDmanager (Jan 2026) reports DRP as ~154k, so cite DRP component as approximate.

claim_as_stated: USFS and NPS each lost >25% of employees Sep 2024-Jan 2026; park rangers -34.1%; under-30 share of federal workforce 7.9%.
correct_statement: Per PPS analysis of OPM data, USFS and NPS each lost more than a quarter of employees Sep 2024-Jan 2026; park rangers fell 34.1%; under-30 share fell from 8.9% (Sep 2024) to 7.9% (Jan 2026).
source_title: The Federal Workforce One Year into the Trump Administration (Fed Figures)
note: PPS gives no exact USFS/NPS percentages. Other sources use different bases (e.g., FH-035 cites USDA OIG: USFS lost 16% in 2025); do not mix them.

claim_as_stated: EPA staff fell to ~12,849 (approx. -24%); median service of departing EPA staff ~30.3 years.
correct_statement: EPA had 12,849 employees at end of Jan 2026 (OPM data analyzed by Inside Climate News), a loss of more than 4,000 (24%) in the first year of the administration. The 30.3-year median service applies to the nearly 2,000 employees who left at year-end 2025 (vs 10.8 years for remaining staff), not to all 2025 departures.
source_title: EPA Hits 40-Year Lows in Staffing After Trump Targets Its Public Health Experts
note: Secondary analysis of OPM data (news). Scope the 30.3-year figure to year-end departures.

claim_as_stated: USFS hired no non-fire seasonal employees in 2025 and committed to ~2,000 for 2026.
correct_statement: Per a Mar 18, 2026 letter from Reps. Neguse and Huffman relaying agency information: with the exception of fire-related positions, USFS did not hire seasonal staff in 2025 due to budget constraints, and on Feb 12, 2026 committed to hiring 2,000 seasonals for 2026 (announced by Secretary Rollins).
source_title: Neguse, Huffman press US Forest Service for answers on staffing levels ahead of summer
note: No USDA/USFS primary press release located; announcement corroborated by press (WoodCentral 2026-02-16 citing Rollins/Schultz). Cite as congressional letter relaying agency statements.

claim_as_stated: AmeriCorps cuts of ~$400M hit conservation corps; FY2026 AmeriCorps status (settlement/stay to Feb 1, 2027).
correct_statement: In April 2025 AmeriCorps terminated nearly $400M in grants, hitting conservation corps. On Jun 5, 2025 Judge Boardman (D. Md.) preliminarily enjoined the cuts only in the 24 plaintiff states + DC; terminated programs there were reinstated and OMB released $184M+ in withheld funds (Aug 2025). A Sep 11, 2026 settlement with 23 AGs and two governors: AmeriCorps does not anticipate FY2026 mass grant terminations or member dismissals, must give 30 days notice of such actions, must commit substantially all FY2026 funds by Sep 30, 2026; litigation stayed through Feb 1, 2027.
source_title: Attorney General Ellison wins settlement blocking Trump Administration from dismantling AmeriCorps; Judge orders Trump administration to restore AmeriCorps as litigation continues
source_publisher: Minnesota Attorney General's Office; Maryland Matters
note: Stop presenting the $400M as a standing cut: it was largely reinstated in plaintiff jurisdictions; cuts persisted in non-plaintiff states. Settlement binds only to FY2026 and the coalition.

claim_as_stated: The U.S. Wildland Fire Service was established at DOI in January 2026, consolidating bureau fire programs (incl. BIA); ~5,780 federal + ~900 Tribal fire personnel.
correct_statement: SO 3448 (Jan 12, 2026) established the U.S. Wildland Fire Service at DOI (directed by SO 3443, Sep 10, 2025), unifying the fire programs of BIA, BLM, NPS and FWS plus the Office of Wildland Fire and Office of Aviation Services. DOI states USWFS employs 5,780 federal wildland fire personnel annually and supports ~900 Tribal wildland fire personnel.
source_title: About the U.S. Wildland Fire Service; SO 3448 - Establishment of the U.S. Wildland Fire Service
note: USFS fire was NOT moved; consolidation of USFS fire is only proposed in the FY2027 budget (TN-011). Tribal personnel are supported, not employed (ISDEAA programs).

claim_as_stated: USDA/USFS reorganization: HQ to Salt Lake City; nine regional offices closing; 57 of 77 research facilities closing; relocations through 2027.
correct_statement: Announced Mar 31-Apr 1, 2026: USFS HQ moves from Washington to Salt Lake City (~260 staff; ~130 remain in DC); all nine regional offices close in a shift to a state-based model with 15 state directors (facilities in R6 Portland, R8 Atlanta, R9 Milwaukee shut); 57 of 77 research facilities in 31 states close; relocations run from summer 2026 into 2027.
source_title: Forest Service to move HQ out of DC, shutter regional offices in sweeping overhaul; Forest Service will close research stations that study wildfire risk (AP)
source_publisher: Government Executive; AP via Hawaii Tribune-Herald
note: Press reports based on Chief Schultz email and internal memos; USDA news release referenced but not read. Implementation status after Jul 2026 not re-checked.

claim_as_stated: EO 14356 (Oct 15, 2025) created agency Strategic Hiring Committees approving every vacancy, with annual staffing plans.
correct_statement: EO 14356, Ensuring Continued Accountability in Federal Hiring (signed Oct 15, 2025), requires each agency to set up a Strategic Hiring Committee (deputy head, chief of staff, others) within 30 days that approves the creation or filling of each vacancy, and annual staffing plans (first within 60 days, then each fiscal year) coordinated with OPM and OMB, with quarterly updates from FY2026 Q2. Exceptions include immigration enforcement, national security and public safety. No sunset.
source_title: Executive Order 14356: Ensuring Continued Accountability in Federal Hiring
note: The EO sets no hiring ratio; the 1-for-4 ratio applies via OPM/OMB guidance (Nov 5, 2025) until plans are submitted. OPM issued further Guidance on Annual Staffing Plans on Jul 30, 2026.

claim_as_stated: OPM Merit Hiring Plan (May 29, 2025); self-assessment questionnaires may not rank candidates after Sep 30, 2025; technical-assessment adoption rates (91% self-report-only in FY2025; 34.3% technical by FY2026 Q2).
correct_statement: OPM issued the Merit Hiring Plan May 29, 2025. From Sep 30, 2025 agencies may use self-assessment questionnaires only for minimum qualifications/eligibility, not rating and ranking (exceptions: seasonal, GS-04 and below, OPM-authorized). In FY2025, 91.23% (41,386) of delegated examining (DE) announcements relied solely on self-report questionnaires; in FY2026 Q2, 34.3% of DE announcements used technical and/or off-the-shelf assessments.
source_title: Chance to Compete Act of 2024 Consolidated Report to Congress; CTCA Governmentwide Implementation Plan for Transition to Technical Assessments
note: Both percentages are for delegated examining announcements only, not all hiring. Essay Q3 stayed in AFGE v. Kupor (Sep 2026; FH-032).

claim_as_stated: OPM Phase One occupational series consolidation memo (Apr 24, 2026): 115 series; 0410/0437/0480/0487->0401; 0455->0404; 0029->0303; 0688->0601.
correct_statement: OPM CHCO memo Modernization and Consolidation of Occupational Series (Apr 24, 2026; V. Hinton) issued a PROPOSED Phase One list of 115 series (~4,926 employees) for realignment, incl. 0410/0437/0480/0487->0401, 0455->0404, 0029->0303, 0688->0601 (also 0023->0186, 0190->0101, 0459->4701, 0698->0640, 0965->0901, 1372/1380->1301, 1374->1311). Agency feedback due May 11, 2026; OPM to finalize decisions after review. No final-decision memo appears on the CHCO published-memos index as of Oct 23, 2026.
source_title: Modernization and Consolidation of Occupational Series (CHCO memo)
note: Say "proposed for realignment", not "consolidated". Final status not confirmed; agencies could request retention.

claim_as_stated: OPM issued competency-based classification and qualification standards for 2210 on Apr 13, 2026 under the Federal Workforce Competency Initiative (FWCI); targets of 300+ / 600+ series.
correct_statement: On Apr 13, 2026 OPM issued four CHCO memos: competency-based position classification standard and qualification standard for 2210, job aids, and FWCI General and Technical Competencies and Competency Frameworks (FWCI survey memo followed Apr 27). OPM's Dec 2025 CTCA report targets updating 300+ GS series by end of FY2026 and an additional 300+ (600+ total) by end of FY2027.
source_title: CHCO Council Published Memos index; Chance to Compete Act of 2024 Consolidated Report to Congress
note: As of Oct 23, 2026 the CHCO index lists competency-based standards only for 2210; the FY2026 300+ target appears not met via published memos (memo index only; not proof).

claim_as_stated: Schedule Policy/Career final rule (Feb 6, 2026; effective Mar 9, 2026) and a June 2026 EO moving ~8,000 employees.
correct_statement: OPM final rule Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (RIN 3206-AO80; 91 FR 5580) published Feb 6, 2026, effective Mar 9, 2026. EO 14410, Implementing Schedule Policy/Career in the Excepted Service, signed Jun 3, 2026 (published Jun 10, 2026), placed positions listed in its appendix into Schedule Policy/Career; press and Lawfare analysis put this at ~8,000 employees in ~4,800 positions across 54 agencies (97% GS-15 or above).
source_title: Improving Performance, Accountability and Responsiveness in the Civil Service (final rule); Executive Order 14410
source_publisher: OPM (Federal Register); Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents
note: The ~8,000 figure is not in the EO text (appendix); cite MeriTalk/Lawfare for it. Litigation pending (PEER, AFGE, NTEU, GAP).

claim_as_stated: OPM memo of Aug 27, 2026 on AI use in hiring (AI-drafted PDs generally not high-impact when humans adopt them).
correct_statement: OPM memo Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Federal Hiring Process (Aug 27, 2026; Director Kupor) treats drafting job-opportunity artifacts incl. position descriptions as generally not high-impact under M-25-21 when drafting does not affect access to employment and the responsible official independently reviews, revises and adopts the draft; adoption without substantive documented review is high-impact. Rating/ranking/scoring is presumed high-impact. 5 CFR 300.103 job analysis applies; applicant data only in agency-authorized tools.
source_title: Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Federal Hiring Process (CHCO memo)
note: Memo states these are OPM views developed with OMB, not official OMB determinations; agencies make their own M-25-21 determinations.

claim_as_stated: Conservation job postings fell 29.4% YoY (Mar-Sep 2025); paid internships -43.8%; AmeriCorps postings -42%.
correct_statement: Postings on the Conservation Job Board fell 29.4% year over year for Mar 1-Sep 30, 2025; paid internships fell 43.8% and AmeriCorps positions 42% (with a survey of 337 conservation employers).
source_title: Analysis Of Conservation Job Postings Shows Significant Decrease During 2025
note: Scope is one job board, not the whole conservation labor market; analyst not named in the article.

claim_as_stated: FY2026 Interior-Environment appropriations approx. $42.56bn (-1.9% YoY), well above the President's request.
correct_statement: FY2026 Interior-Environment appropriations enacted in P.L. 119-74, Division C (Jan 23, 2026) total $42.56bn, down $809M (1.9%) from FY2025 ($43.37bn), vs a President's request of $26.85bn. Total includes $2.85bn wildfire suppression cap adjustment and $5.31bn IHS FY2027 advance appropriations. USFS $8.61bn (request $2.31bn); NPS $3.27bn; EPA $8.82bn.
source_title: Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies: Overview of FY2026 Appropriations (R48726)

claim_as_stated: Federal Workforce Data (data.opm.gov) replaced FedScope (Jan 2026).
correct_statement: OPM launched the Federal Workforce Data (FWD) site at data.opm.gov in Jan 2026, replacing FedScope, with monthly data updates.
source_title: OPM Launches New Workforce Data Site; New federal workforce data site goes live with more current information
source_publisher: U.S. Office of Personnel Management; FEDweek
note: Release lists retirement eligibility, telework, admin leave, performance ratings and hiring activity; series-level content not described in the release.

claim_as_stated: Natural Resources Management named a Tier 2 occupational group for Chance to Compete technical assessments, full implementation FY2028.
correct_statement: OPM's July 2026 CTCA implementation plan places Natural Resources Management in Tier 2 (Medium Priority, with Transportation and Physical Sciences), addressed after Tier 1 (IT, Accounting and Budget, Legal) matures. No Tier 2 completion date is given; FY2028 is the governmentwide full-implementation target tied to the final (Tier 3) phase.
source_title: Chance to Compete Act of 2024 Governmentwide Implementation Plan for Transition to Technical Assessments (Report to Congress)
note: Report is internally inconsistent (transition "by the end of 2027" vs full implementation end of FY2028). Do not say NRM will be fully implemented by FY2028 specifically.

claim_as_stated: CEQ's NEPA regulations were removed (interim final rule 2025; final removal effective Jan 8, 2026?) and agencies adopted their own procedures (DOI handbook; USDA 7 CFR 1b).
stated_by: statecraft (PI-NEPA-02, PI-NEPA-04, PI-NEPA-05; SC-009, SC-011, SC-014)
correct_statement: CEQ's interim final rule (90 FR 10610, Feb 25, 2025; effective Apr 11, 2025) removed 40 CFR parts 1500-1508; CEQ adopted it as final without change at 91 FR 618 (Jan 8, 2026), effective Jan 8, 2026. CEQ reasons it may lack authority to issue binding rules after EO 14154 revoked EO 11991. Agencies follow their own procedures (CEQ guidance/template 90 FR 47734, Oct 2, 2025). DOI final rule 91 FR 8738 (Feb 24, 2026; effective same day) keeps a slimmed 43 CFR part 46 and moves most procedures to the 'Department of the Interior Handbook: National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures'. USDA final rule (published and effective Apr 3, 2026) consolidates USDA procedures in 7 CFR part 1b and rescinds 36 CFR part 220 (Forest Service) in full; applies to CEs immediately, EAs published after May 18, 2026 and EISs with NOI after Jul 2, 2026.
source_title: Removal of National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations (final rule); National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Regulations (DOI final rule); National Environmental Policy Act (USDA final rule, FR Doc 2026-06537)
source_publisher: Council on Environmental Quality (Federal Register); Department of the Interior (Federal Register); USDA (Federal Register public inspection); WilmerHale client alert
note: Drop the question mark: Jan 8, 2026 effective date confirmed. Do not call the DOI handbook '516 DM 1' (the final rule names it the DOI NEPA Handbook; 516 DM is cited only as where pre-2008 procedures lived). USDA FR page: statecraft cites 91 FR 17092, WilmerHale cites 91 FR 17,062; page not confirmed from primary - cite by date and FR Doc 2026-06537 until checked.

claim_as_stated: Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (May 2025) - 'substantial deference' to agency NEPA judgments.
correct_statement: Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County, No. 23-975, decided May 29, 2025: Kavanaugh for the Court (Roberts, Thomas, Alito, Barrett); Sotomayor concurred in the judgment (Kagan, Jackson); Gorsuch did not participate. The D.C. Circuit 'failed to afford the Board the substantial judicial deference required in NEPA cases'; agencies need not analyze effects of separate upstream/downstream projects; 'NEPA requires agencies to focus on the environmental effects of the project at issue.'
source_title: Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County (opinion text)
source_publisher: Supreme Court of the United States (via Cornell LII)
note: Statecraft's '(5-3)' is misleading: judgment was 8-0 (reversed and remanded); the majority opinion had 5 votes and 3 concurred in the judgment. Say '8-0 judgment; 5-justice majority opinion'. U.S. Reports cite 605 U.S. 168 not shown on fetched page.

claim_as_stated: SPEED Act passed the House (Dec 18, 2025); current Senate status; key provisions (150-day limitations period; standing tied to substantive comments).
correct_statement: H.R. 4776 (SPEED Act, Rep. Westerman) passed the House 221-196 on Dec 18, 2025 (Roll Call 356); same day received in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works. No later Senate action is recorded (latest action Dec 18, 2025); not enacted. As passed: claims generally barred unless filed within 150 days of publication of final agency action; where a comment period occurred, only parties that submitted a 'substantive and unique comment' may sue; remand is the sole remedy, with the action left in effect during a 180-day cure period; 'substantial deference' codified; effects limited to those with a 'reasonably close causal relationship' to the project.
source_title: H.R. 4776 timeline (congressional record data); SPEED Act Passes House (Law and the Environment blog)
source_publisher: The Lobby News (Congress.gov data mirror); Foley Hoag LLP
note: Status taken from a Congress.gov data mirror; re-check congress.gov immediately before publication. Separate Senate bill S. 3224 (statecraft) not checked. Describe as 'passed House; pending in Senate EPW', not as law.

claim_as_stated: NEPA s.112 sponsor-funded expedited reviews (180-day EA / 1-year EIS) - status and use.
correct_statement: NEPA section 112, added by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (Pub. L. 119-21, signed Jul 4, 2025), lets a project sponsor pay a fee of 125% of the anticipated cost of preparing or supervising the document in exchange for deadlines of 180 days for an EA (from fee payment) and 1 year for an EIS (from the NOI). Sponsors submit a project description and a declaration on whether they will prepare the document under NEPA s.107(f) to CEQ, which must set the fee within 15 days. The provision is in force; CEQ maintains an intake page on nepa.gov.
source_title: Section 112 NEPA Project Sponsor Opt-In Fees; The One Big Beautiful Bill Act Offers Expedited NEPA Review for a Fee
source_publisher: Council on Environmental Quality (nepa.gov); O'Melveny & Myers
note: Use: no public count or list of projects using s.112 found (not-found for the 'use' half). The CEQ page does not state the 125% figure; it comes from the statute as summarized by counsel. The claim that s.112 does not speed ESA/NHPA reviews is a reasonable reading (the section covers only NEPA documents) but was not confirmed in a source this pass.

claim_as_stated: ESA 'harm' definition rescission - final? effective date; litigation.
correct_statement: Final. FWS and NMFS published 'Rescinding the Definition of Harm Under the Endangered Species Act' at 91 FR 43300 (Jul 14, 2026; FR Doc 2026-14195), amending 50 CFR parts 17 and 222; effective Sep 14, 2026 (proposed Apr 17, 2025, 90 FR 16102). Habitat modification alone is no longer 'take' under s.9; standards are prospective only (prior permits/ITSs need not be reevaluated); s.7 adverse-modification duties and critical habitat designations are unchanged. Litigation: nine conservation groups (CBD, Sierra Club, WildEarth Guardians and others; Earthjustice counsel) and, separately, the Swinomish Indian Tribal Community sued in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington in mid-July 2026 (complaint dated Jul 14, 2026).
source_title: Rescinding the Definition of Harm Under the Endangered Species Act (final rule); WA tribes, environmental groups sue over Endangered Species Act rule change
source_publisher: FWS and NMFS (Federal Register); Idaho Capital Sun / Washington State Standard
note: Correct statecraft's effective date from 2026-09-12 to 2026-09-14 and its 'notice of intent to sue 2026-07-15' to 'suits filed in W.D. Wash. mid-July 2026'. CBD complaint PDF (biologicaldiversity.org, 07-14-2026) seen in search results, not opened. Case outcome not checked.

claim_as_stated: EPA GHG endangerment finding rescission - final? date; litigation.
correct_statement: Final. 'Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle Greenhouse Gas Emission Standards Under the Clean Air Act', 91 FR 7686 (published Feb 18, 2026; finalized Feb 12, 2026); effective Apr 20, 2026. EPA concludes CAA s.202(a)(1) does not authorize GHG regulation in response to global climate change (best reading plus major questions doctrine) and repeals all federal vehicle/engine GHG standards. Litigation in the D.C. Circuit: No. 26-1037 (filed Feb 18, 2026 by 17 health and environmental groups) and No. 26-1061 (filed Mar 19, 2026 by NY, MA, CA, CT AGs joined by 24 states plus cities, counties, DC); reconsideration petition to EPA filed Apr 16, 2026; motions to defer merits briefing were lodged.
source_title: Rescission of the Greenhouse Gas Endangerment Finding and Motor Vehicle GHG Emission Standards (final rule); Challenges to EPA's Repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding
note: Statecraft's case names (APHA v. EPA; 'Bay Area AQMD v. EPA, filed 2026-04-16') were not confirmed; Apr 16, 2026 matches the administrative reconsideration petition, not a court filing. Use docket numbers above. Merits status after June 2026 not checked.

claim_as_stated: WOTUS rule status (2025-26 proposal/final).
correct_statement: No final rule as of Oct 2026. EPA and the Army proposed a revised WOTUS definition implementing Sackett v. EPA (FR Doc 2025-20402, Nov 20, 2025), which is pending. A more restrictive supplemental proposal (FR Doc 2026-18317) was published Sep 9, 2026, with comments due Oct 9, 2026; it floats interpretations of Sackett terms ('relatively permanent, standing, or continuously flowing'). The amended 2023 (conforming) rule is the baseline the proposals would narrow.
source_title: WOTUS Supplemental Proposed Rule (Quick Take)
source_publisher: Harvard Law School Environmental & Energy Law Program
note: Statecraft dates the supplemental 'announced 2026-09-04'; FR publication is Sep 9, 2026 (announcement date not confirmed). The '>220,000 comments; closed 2026-01-05' figures were not confirmed this pass. State-by-state applicability of the 2023 rule vs pre-2015 regime (due to injunctions) not checked; do not generalize.

claim_as_stated: CEQ permitting technology: data standard version (v1.2.0?), Permitting Technology Action Plan, PermitAI/NEPATEC.
correct_statement: CEQ's NEPA and Permitting Data and Technology Standard is at Version 1.2, published Aug 18, 2025 (no newer version shown on the Permitting Innovation Center page; technical resources in GitHub GSA-TTS/pic-standards). CEQ issued the Permitting Technology Action Plan on May 30, 2025, implementing the Apr 15, 2025 Presidential Memorandum 'Updating Permitting Technology for the 21st Century' (minimum functional requirements, initial data standard, roadmap, governance); CEQ-led Permitting Innovation Center with GSA TTS. PNNL PermitAI offers reusable modules (SearchNEPA, CommentNEPA, WriteNEPA, EngageNEPA, PermitCE, PermitReg, PermitLex) and the NEPATEC corpus, funded by DOE offices and the Permitting Council; PNNL and OpenAI released DraftNEPABench (102 test cases from 19 agencies), presented May 27-29, 2026; SearchNEPA is available to federal NEPA reviewers.
source_title: NEPA and Permitting Data and Technology Standard; Trump Administration Launches Permitting Technology Action Plan; PermitAI project page; PermitAI public-private partnership speeds environmental review drafting tasks
source_publisher: CEQ Permitting Innovation Center; The White House; Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
note: Say 'v1.2', not 'v1.2.0'. CC0 licence not stated on the standard page (check GitHub repo). Not confirmed: 'NEPATEC 3.0 released Aug 2026', production/beta status of each module, and the '1-5 hours saved per EIS subsection (up to ~15%)' figure - PNNL's release gives only qualitative results and inconsistent corpus counts (120,000+ vs 140,000+ documents). Do not publish those numbers without the paper.

claim_as_stated: OMB M-25-21 and M-25-22 (Apr 2025) on federal AI use and acquisition; M-26-04 (LLM procurement) and M-26-05 (secure software, rescinding M-22-18/M-23-16), Jan 2026.
stated_by: compliance-product (CR-04, CR-17, CR-18; CP-014, CP-021, CP-023, CP-024); data-craft
correct_statement: M-25-21 ('Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust') and M-25-22 ('Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government') were issued Apr 3, 2025, replacing M-24-10 and M-24-18; M-25-22 applies to contracts from solicitations issued about 180 days after issuance (late Sep/Oct 1, 2025) and requires contracts to bar training publicly or commercially available AI on non-public agency data without explicit consent. M-26-04 ('Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles', implementing EO 14319) is dated Dec 11, 2025 - not Jan 2026; it requires LLM solicitations to include contractual terms (acceptable use policy; model, system and/or data cards; end-user resources; feedback mechanism), agency procurement policy updates by Mar 11, 2026, exempts free open-source LLMs (due diligence still expected) and sunsets two years after issuance unless extended. M-26-05 ('Adopting a Risk-based Approach to Software and Hardware Security') is dated Jan 23, 2026 and rescinds M-22-18 and M-23-16; agencies keep software/hardware inventories and set risk-based assurance policies; the CISA attestation form becomes optional; agencies may require an SBOM on request.
source_title: M-26-04 (PDF); M-26-05 (PDF); White House Issues Guidance on Use and Procurement of AI Technology
source_publisher: Office of Management and Budget; Ropes & Gray
note: Only the key-fact phrasing is wrong: M-26-04 is December 2025 (compliance-product CR-18 already has Dec 11, 2025). Call M-26-04 'Unbiased AI Principles for LLM procurement', not a general LLM-procurement memo. M-25-21/22 PDFs themselves not opened this pass (see CP-036).

claim_as_stated: FedRAMP 20x and the 'Consolidated Rules for 2026' (certification classes; dates).
correct_statement: FedRAMP's Consolidated Rules for 2026 (CR26) replace 'authorization' with 'certification' (to avoid confusion with agency ATOs) and define Class A (new transitional class), Class B (formerly Low), Class C (formerly Moderate) and Class D (formerly High). FedRAMP's official 2026 timeline: Jul 4, 2026 optional early adoption; Jul 6, 2026 Initial Implementation marketplace listings; Jul 28, 2026 FedRAMP Ready becomes legacy (no new submissions; pursue 20x Class A); Aug 3, 2026 20x Class A pipeline opens; Aug 10, 2026 temporary Rev5 Program Certification pipelines (Class B/C; Ready Conversion and Lost Sponsor - no agency sponsor needed); Aug 31, 2026 20x Class B and C pipeline opens; Jan 1, 2027 mandatory adoption for all stakeholders; Jun 11, 2027 no new Rev5 certification applications accepted.
source_title: FedRAMP 2026 Timeline; FedRAMP Releases Its Consolidated Rules for 2026
note: FedRAMP labels Jul 4, 2026 'Optional Early Adoption'; DWT describes it as effective for new 20x certifications - say 'available from Jul 4, 2026; mandatory Jan 1, 2027'. The vendor dates in CP-019 (Class A Aug 3; B/C Aug 31; Ready retired Jul 28) match the official timeline, so cite fedramp.gov instead of Knox Systems. 'Launched June 24, 2026' and 'Class A presumed adequate for processing public information' not confirmed this pass; no Class D pipeline date is published.

claim_as_stated: DOJ ADA Title II web accessibility deadlines moved to Apr 26, 2027 / Apr 26, 2028 (interim final rule, Apr 2026); WCAG 2.1 AA.
stated_by: compliance-product (CP-012, CP-013; report and compliance matrix)
correct_statement: DOJ interim final rule 'Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities', 91 FR 20902 (published and effective Apr 20, 2026; comments closed Jun 22, 2026) amends 28 CFR 35.200(b): public entities with total population 50,000+ must comply by Apr 26, 2027 (was Apr 24, 2026); entities under 50,000 and special district governments by Apr 26, 2028 (was Apr 26, 2027). The technical standard remains WCAG 2.1 Level AA; no other provision of the 2024 rule changed. DOJ signals a possible future proposed rule on the 2024 rule's substance.
source_title: Extension of Compliance Dates for Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability; Accessibility of Web Information and Services of State and Local Government Entities (interim final rule)
source_publisher: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division (Federal Register)
note: Watch item: DOJ says it may propose substantive changes to the 2024 rule, so WCAG 2.1 AA is the current standard but not guaranteed to stay.

claim_as_stated: WCAG 2.2 published as ISO/IEC 40500:2025.
correct_statement: W3C announced on Oct 21, 2025 that WCAG 2.2 was approved as international standard ISO/IEC 40500:2025.
source_title: WCAG 2.2 Approved as an ISO Standard
note: The announcement does not state what it supersedes (ISO/IEC 40500:2012 was WCAG 2.0) or anything about WCAG 2.3/3 timing; compliance-product's 'there will be no 2.3' and 'WCAG 3 draft Sep 2026' rest on other sources not re-checked here.

claim_as_stated: EO 13175 still in effect; EO 14112 rescinded; status of Joint Secretarial Order 3403 and federal Indigenous Knowledge guidance; DOI 301 DM 7.
stated_by: tribal-sovereignty (report; TN-018, TN-026, TN-027); statecraft (PI-TRIBE-01; SC-035, SC-036)

claim_as_stated: Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen 'Canaries in the Coal Mine?' (2025): early-career employment in AI-exposed occupations; 2026 follow-ups. Team: 22-25-year-olds in the two most-exposed quintiles ~19% below counterfactual by June 2026, up from 15% at the July 2025 vintage, via reduced hiring.
correct_statement: Stanford Digital Economy Lab, Aug 12, 2026: 'No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%'. Employment of 22-25-year-olds in highly AI-exposed occupations is ~19% below the less-exposed trend as of June 2026 (15% at the July 2025 vintage). Their employment in the two most-exposed quintiles fell ~11% Nov 2022-Jun 2026, while the three least-exposed grew ~10%. The adjustment comes mainly through reduced hiring and shows in employment, not base pay. No economy-wide displacement was found, and there is no comparable gap for experienced workers. The revised paper is 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence' (Aug 2026 revision), which adds codified vs tacit knowledge. Follow-ups: the ADP Research/Stanford Canaries Dashboard (monthly), the Stanford AI Economic Indicators project, and the Feb 2026 post on interest rates and timing.
source_title: No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%
note: Patterns are descriptive, not causal. Gaps shrink with education controls, and estimates exceed national survey benchmarks. The often-quoted 2025 '13% relative decline' figure comes from the Aug 2025 paper version and is superseded; use 15% (Jul 2025 vintage) to 19% (Jun 2026).

claim_as_stated: ILO generative-AI exposure index: latest refinement (2025) and headline (ISCO-08 task-level exposure gradients with expert validation).
